title: Your Doorframe Pull Test Reveals the Truth About Your back nerve drive
description: Grip a doorframe, lean back, and row. The number of strict reps before your back gives up measures the nerve drive into the biggest muscles you own. Here is why backs sleep through training, and how a doorframe wakes them up.

scenes.narration: Find a doorframe. | Grip both sides, | chest height, firm. | Feet close to the wall, | body straight as a plank. | Lean back until | your arms are straight. | Now pull your chest | to the frame. | Squeeze the shoulder blades. | Lower with control. | That is one rep. | Count the strict ones. | No hip swinging. | No half reps. | When your back gives up | and your arms take over, | the test is over. | That rep count | is your DRIVE score. | Keep it safe. | At the | end of this video | I will tell you | what it says | about your back.

beats.title: WHEN ARMS TAKE OVER
lines: The back has left the set.

scenes.label: STRICT DOORFRAME ROWS
scenes.sub: under 6: the back drive is asleep - 15 plus: a wired, working back
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Twelve strict doorframe rows, chest to frame, blades squeezed, is a back whose nerve drive is awake and working. Six to twelve is the building middle: the lats fire, but they tire and delegate to the arms early. Under six, and especially if your biceps burned more than your back, the drive into your back is asleep, and it has probably been asleep through every row and pull-down you have ever done. Do not blame the muscles. The lats are the biggest sheet of muscle in your upper body. When they underperform, the signal is the suspect, every time.

Why do backs sleep? Because you cannot see them. Your nervous system builds its control maps from feedback, and the back is the one major region you have never watched work in a mirror. So the brain runs it on autopilot: vague, low-resolution, easily hijacked by the arms, which it can see and trusts. The result is a movement pattern where the elbows bend and the load moves, but the lats, the actual target, contribute a fraction of what they own. DRIVE is the fixable variable: the strength and specificity of the signal into the back. Doorframe rows are the perfect classroom for it, because the load is modest, the position is fixed, and you can spend the whole set doing one thing: pulling from the elbows, feeling the blades travel, making the back the author of every rep.

The training science here is the same recruitment story from the activation episode, aimed at the biggest muscles you have. A stronger, more specific signal recruits more of the lat's fibres, including the high-threshold ones that only answer strong orders. Those fibres are where pulling strength and back thickness live. Isometric pauses at the chest, two full seconds of maximum blade squeeze per rep, are the fastest drive builder known, because a pause removes momentum and forces the signal to do all the work. Studies of pause training keep showing the same thing: the pause rep teaches more per rep than the moving rep. Five paused reps will wake a back that fifty sloppy reps put to sleep.

beats.title: THE PAUSE TEACHES
lines: The signal does all the work.

scenes.narration: Underneath drive sits a smaller skill worth isolating: the shoulder blades themselves. Every row is two movements wearing one coat, the blades gliding together and apart across the ribcage, and the arm bending at the elbow. When the blade movement is stiff or unmapped, the arm movement dominates and the back spectates. Wall slides, the same drill the healing season used, are blade school: slow, loaded glides that teach the blades to travel. Spend two weeks sliding daily and your rows will feel different before they get stronger, because the platform the lats pull from finally moves properly. Drive needs a road. The blades are the road.

Set your geometry honestly, because doorframe rows scale beautifully when you respect the dial. Feet further from the wall and a deeper lean make every rep heavier; feet closer and a shallower lean make it lighter. The test only counts at the angle where your body stays a true plank and the chest reaches the frame. As your drive builds over the month, the progression is not more cheating reps at the same angle. It is the same strict reps at a deeper lean, then single-arm rows, then rows with a three-second pause. Write your test angle down next to your number. An unrecorded angle makes the retest meaningless, and meaningless retests are how people convince themselves nothing works.

Now the skinny advantage, | and it is structural. | A row moves your body. | Less body, less load | per rep at any angle. | That sounds easier. | It is actually better. | Drive training needs | reps you fully own, | where the back, | not survival, decides. | The heavy guy's rows | degrade into arm pulls | by rep five. | Yours stay strict | deep into the set. | Every strict rep | is a drive lesson. | You get more lessons | per session, | per week, per month. | That is | how backs wake up.
Train with me. Same frame, same lean as your test. Pull, pause two seconds at the chest, lower slowly. Forty seconds on, twenty off, three rounds. The back works, the arms just hold. Go.

Your week: doorframe rows three days, always with the two-second chest pause, sets stopped the moment the arms start authoring reps. One day, add the activation drill from episode two of this season: maximum lat squeezes, ten per side, imagining the elbows dragging down and back. Three mistakes keep backs asleep. Pulling with the hands instead of driving the elbows. Letting the hips sag so the plank becomes a hammock. And progressing by leaning deeper before the current angle is strict, which trades drive lessons for survival reps. If rowing brings sharp shoulder pain, a pinching at the front of the shoulder, or elbow pain that lingers for days, see a professional if it persists. Drive should burn between the shoulder blades, nowhere else.

beats.text: DRIVE THE ELBOWS, NOT THE HANDS

scenes.narration: So, your number. Under six strict reps, or a set your biceps remember better than your back: your back drive is asleep, and waking it is the single highest-value project in your training right now. Six to twelve: the lats are answering, and pauses will make them fluent. Fifteen or more at a true plank angle: your back is wired, and single-arm work is your next country. Record the reps and the lean angle together. Retest in thirty days at the identical angle, and put both numbers in the comments. A back that authors its own reps changes every pull you will ever do. Film your retest set from behind if you can. The video will show you the moment the blades start travelling like they mean it, and that picture is worth more than the rep count. Keep the frame, the lean and the standard identical, always.

Thirty days of paused, strict pulling and that doorframe becomes a measuring instrument for a waking back. Pull from the elbows, pause, and let the big muscles work. Subscribe so the retest finds you. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
